lead: A turbocharger that cannot change its turbine area is a compromise: small enough for low-speed response, or large enough for high-speed power, never both. A variable geometry turbocharger moves vanes or a nozzle ring to change the area while running. An intercooler then removes the heat that compression added, so the charge is denser at the same boost. Together they give strong low-speed torque, controlled high-speed boost and lower NOx. They appear in diesel cars, trucks, tractors and some petrol engines.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.6 for pressure ratio, compressor heating and the turbine side; Chapter 4.5 for why boost adds air mass.

blocks.text: A fixed turbine has one inlet area. At 1200 rpm the exhaust flow is small, gas speed through the nozzle is low, and the turbine extracts little work. The compressor therefore makes little boost. At 5000 rpm the same area is too small. Exhaust backs up in the cylinder, pumping loss rises, and boost may exceed the limit. A variable geometry turbocharger (VGT) changes the turbine inlet area while the engine runs.

items: Moving vanes: small vanes pivot at the nozzle throat. Closed vanes give a narrow throat and high gas speed at low flow.
Sliding nozzle ring: an axial ring moves to cover or open the throat. It gives the same area change with fewer moving parts.
Actuator: a vacuum capsule or electric motor moves the vanes or ring. The ECU uses engine speed, fuel quantity, boost pressure and vane position to set the area.
Low speed: small area, high exhaust velocity, fast spool. High speed: large area, low back pressure, boost held at the map limit.

blocks.text: The result is boost at 1200 rpm that a fixed turbine cannot reach. In the figure the fixed unit is near 0.2 bar there, while the VGT is near 0.9 bar. The actuator is the weak point in cost and reliability. It lives near hot exhaust, so position feedback and self-calibration matter.

A wastegate is a valve that bypasses exhaust around the turbine to cap boost. It cannot make the turbine smaller at low speed, so it does not fix lag. VGT controls boost by area, so it often needs no wastegate. It also raises exhaust temperature and flow for exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), and it can close the vanes to create back pressure for an exhaust brake on a downhill run.

Compression heats the charge. For a perfect gas, density ρ = p/(R T). The compressor raises p by the pressure ratio r<sub>p</sub>, but it also raises T, so density rises by less than r<sub>p</sub>. At pressure ratio 1.6 and compressor efficiency 0.70, the air leaves at about 362 K instead of 300 K. The density ratio is 1.33, not 1.60. An intercooler is a heat exchanger between the compressor and the intake manifold. It removes heat at nearly constant pressure.

blocks.where: ε is intercooler effectiveness (0 to 1); T<sub>2</sub> is compressor outlet temperature in K; T<sub>3</sub> is intercooler outlet temperature in K; T<sub>coolant,in</sub> is cooling air or water inlet temperature in K. A value near 1 means the outlet is close to the coolant inlet temperature.

blocks.text: Air-to-air intercooler uses ram air through a front-mounted core. It is simple and needs no extra pump, but long pipes add volume and throttle lag. Air-to-water intercooler uses a coolant loop and a small radiator. It is compact and holds outlet temperature steady in traffic, but adds mass and a second cooling circuit. In a spark ignition engine the cooler sits before the throttle so only air passes through it. Placing it after the throttle is possible, but the extra volume hurts throttle response.

Intercooling lowers the charge temperature after the compressor. In an SI engine this reduces knock, so the compression ratio or boost can be raised. Volumetric efficiency improves because cold air is denser. Lower peak combustion temperature cuts NOx. Fuel consumption falls at the same power because the ECU can use more air and less fuel enrichment. In a diesel engine the gain is density and NOx control; very cold air can raise ignition delay and particulates, so the cooler is not made larger than needed.

sections.h3: Engine changes that go with boost

blocks.text: Supercharging raises cylinder pressure and temperature. The engine must be built for it. The changes below are common; the exact list depends on boost level and fuel.

head: Part or system
Change
Reason
rows: Less knock at high charge temperature
Larger radiator, oil cooler, turbo feed
Turbo bearing heat and higher engine heat

blocks.text: For a mild boost below 0.5 bar, many of these changes are skipped. For high boost, the block and head gasket are the first limits. The turbocharger needs clean oil at pressure before it spins. A timer or electric auxiliary pump keeps oil flowing after a hot shutdown so the bearing does not coke. The coolant circuit also needs a delay for the same reason.

figure.caption: At 1200 rpm the variable geometry turbine already gives 0.9 bar; the fixed turbine gives 0.2 bar. The two curves meet near 1.3 bar at high speed.

spec.aria: Plot of boost pressure against engine speed comparing a fixed turbine, which is weak at low speed, with a variable geometry turbo that holds boost almost flat from 2000 rpm.

examples.question: A turbocharged engine takes air at 300 K and 1.0 bar. The compressor pressure ratio is 1.6 and its efficiency is 0.70. Take γ = 1.4. Find the compressor outlet temperature, the density ratio without an intercooler, the density ratio when an intercooler cools the charge to 315 K, and the extra air mass.
steps: Density ratio without intercooler = r<sub>p</sub> × T<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>2</sub> = 1.6 × 300/361.7 = 1.327 ≈ 1.33.
Density ratio with intercooler to 315 K = 1.6 × 300/315 = 1.524 ≈ 1.52.
Extra air mass = 1.524/1.327 = 1.148 ≈ 1.15, which is about 15 percent more charge at the same boost.
examples.answer: T<sub>2</sub> ≈ 362 K; density ratio is 1.33 without intercooling and 1.52 with it; the intercooler gives about 1.15 times the air mass, roughly 15 percent more.
examples.check:
T1 = 300.0
p1 = 1.0
rp = 1.6
eta_c = 0.70
gamma = 1.4
T3 = 315.0
exp = (gamma - 1) / gamma
T2 = T1 * (1 + (rp**exp - 1) / eta_c)
dr_no = rp * T1 / T2
dr_ic = rp * T1 / T3
extra = dr_ic / dr_no
print(f'{T2:.0f}')
print(f'{dr_no:.2f}')
print(f'{dr_ic:.2f}')
print(f'{extra:.2f}')

traps: Do not say the intercooler increases boost pressure. It increases density at the same pressure; the pressure ratio is set by the compressor.
VGT vanes close at low engine speed to speed the gas, and open at high speed. Reversing this gives lag and overboost.
A wastegate and a VGT are not the same. A wastegate bypasses exhaust; a VGT changes nozzle area.
Compressor efficiency is in the denominator of the temperature rise term. A lower efficiency gives a hotter outlet, not a cooler one.
Intercooler effectiveness uses the coolant inlet temperature, not the ambient after the radiator or the engine coolant outlet.

quiz.q: What part of a VGT moves to change turbine inlet area?
quiz.a: Moving nozzle vanes or a sliding nozzle ring.

quiz.q: Why does a fixed turbine give weak boost at 1200 rpm?
quiz.a: Exhaust flow is low, so gas speed through the fixed nozzle is low and turbine work is small. The fixed area is too large for that flow.

quiz.q: Compressor inlet is 300 K, pressure ratio is 2.0, compressor efficiency is 0.75 and γ = 1.4. Find the outlet temperature.
Why can an intercooler reduce NOx but increase particulate matter in a diesel engine?
quiz.a: A colder charge lowers peak combustion temperature, so NOx falls. If the charge is too cold, ignition delay lengthens and fuel-air mixing becomes poorer, so soot and particulate matter can rise.

quiz.q: State two differences between a VGT and a wastegate.
quiz.a: A VGT changes turbine inlet area; a wastegate bypasses exhaust gas. A VGT improves low-speed spool; a wastegate mainly caps high-speed boost.

quiz.q: An intercooler has effectiveness 0.8. Compressor outlet is 380 K and cooling air inlet is 300 K. Find the intercooler outlet temperature.
quiz.a: ε = (T<sub>2</sub> − T<sub>3</sub>)/(T<sub>2</sub> − T<sub>coolant,in</sub>). So T<sub>3</sub> = 380 − 0.8(380 − 300) = 316 K.

quiz.q: How does a VGT act as an exhaust brake on a downhill run?
quiz.a: The vanes close to a small area. Exhaust cannot leave easily, so back pressure rises. The engine must pump against this pressure, and that pumping work gives a braking effect.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production diesel cars use electric VGT actuators with closed-loop position control; heavy trucks add two-stage turbocharging and cooled EGR. Research searches: 'variable nozzle turbine hysteresis', 'charge air cooler condensation', 'low-pressure EGR architecture', 'Miller cycle boost'. Hydrogen engines need large charge coolers because knock limits are tight. The same nozzle ideas appear in variable turbine geometry for waste-heat recovery.
